title: Probe: batch coalescence vs starvation — observations & microbenchmark logs
content:
Summary:

This doc captures a set of small, focused experiments to understand when continuous batching (our live scheduler) coalesces requests effectively and when it instead causes request starvation leading to tail-latency spikes. The goal is to find knobs and heuristics that reduce p99/p999 tail without regressing throughput or average latency for mixed workloads.

Motivation / why this felt necessary:
- Several customer incidents in Jan 2025 showed intermittent p999 spikes during low-traffic windows with occasional microbursts.
- Hypothesis: our batch coalescence window + priority rules allow long-lived small requests to wait behind newly arrived high-priority probes, causing starvation for some flows.
- Want to quantify tradeoffs between maximizing batch sizes (costs) and minimizing worst-case latency.

Top-level hypotheses tested:
1) Increasing coalescence window (max_wait_ms) improves throughput and token-per-GPU but increases p999 for low-QPS flows.
2) Age-based promotion (if a request has waited > X ms, force dispatch) reduces p999 at the cost of slightly smaller average batches.
3) Probe isolation (reserve 1 slot per worker for microbursts) prevents head-of-line blocking and reduces tail without hurting steady-state throughput.

Experiment environment and setup:
- Runtime build: serving-runtime@main commit 9f3a2b (batching changes gated behind feature flag "coalesce-probe-v2").
- Hardware: 2x A100-80GB per node (single node runs).
- Configured with standard tracing enabled (zipkin) and tokenized cost accounting.
- Driver workload generated by bench-runner v0.9.1 (internal microbench harness).

Workloads used (representative):
A) Steady mix: 200 qps, 80% small (len 64 tokens), 20% medium (len 512) — baseline for throughput/avg-latency.
B) Low-QPS + microburst: 5 qps background small requests, with periodic 200-RPS microbursts lasting 300ms every 30s (emulates interactive spikes).
C) Many long-latency probes: 50 qps of requests with heavy CPU pre/post processing to create head-of-line risks.

Metrics captured:
- p50/p95/p99/p999 of server-side latency (from arrival to response).
- batching latency (time waited in queue to be assigned to a batch).
- batch size distribution (per-second percentiles).
- throughput (tokens/s and requests/s).
- aborted / dropped requests (should be zero).
- CPU/GPU utilization and kernel launch rates.

Configurations (high level) exercised:
- W0: baseline: max_wait_ms=8, max_batch_tokens=16384, age_promotion=off, reserve_probe_slot=0 (feature-flag off)
- W1: max_wait_ms=20 (+coalescence), age_promotion=off, reserve_probe_slot=0
- W2: max_wait_ms=8, age_promotion=enabled with promote_after_ms=12, reserve_probe_slot=0
- W3: max_wait_ms=8, age_promotion=off, reserve_probe_slot=1 (one reserved slot per worker for microbursts)
- W4: max_wait_ms=12, age_promotion=enabled (promote_after_ms=10), reserve_probe_slot=1 (combined heuristics)

Measurement method and caveats:
- Each config run = 20 minutes steady-state after a 3-minute warmup; repeated 3 times and median reported.
- We sampled spans for p999 diagnosis (span ids included below).
- Caveat: single-node runs underestimate cross-node scheduling noise. Also workload generator and tracing add ~0.3ms overhead.

Key observations (raw findings):
- W1 (longer coalesce window) increased tokens/s by ~9% on workload A but increased p999 by ~1.9x on workload B. Explanation: larger windows accumulate microburst requests which then form large batches but some low-QPS requests wait longer behind the accumulated batch.
- W2 (age-based promotion) kept tokens/s within 2% of baseline for workload A and reduced p999 by ~35% for workload B compared to W0. Very effective for low-QPS starvation scenarios.
- W3 (reserved probe slot) reduced p999 for workload B by ~50% vs W0, with negligible throughput (~0.5% drop) change for workload A. This is promising and cheap to implement.
- W4 (combined) gave the best p999 reduction with only ~3% throughput regression versus W1. It smoothed microburst effects while maintaining improved batching efficiency.

Representative numbers (median of repeats):
Workload B (low-QPS + microbursts):
- W0: p99=42.8ms, p999=198ms, avg batch size=3.1, tokens/s=11.2k
- W1: p99=48.1ms, p999=378ms, avg batch size=5.9, tokens/s=12.2k
- W2: p99=38.9ms, p999=126ms, avg batch size=3.0, tokens/s=11.0k
- W3: p99=36.5ms, p999=98ms, avg batch size=2.9, tokens/s=11.1k
- W4: p99=37.1ms, p999=92ms, avg batch size=4.1, tokens/s=11.8k

Trace-level notes (selected spans):
- span id 0x7a1b3ff: W1 run, snapshot at p999. Shows a request arriving at t=0 queued for 196ms while scheduler kept waiting for coalescing (policy threshold check missed because of priority inversion).
- span id 0x7a24e12: W3 run, same window: shows reserved-slot dispatch for the microburst which allowed the queued low-qps request to dispatch within 28ms.

Root cause analysis (short):
- The scheduler win condition to dispatch aims to hit a token threshold OR last_wait > max_wait_ms. In bursts, new arrivals often satisfy token threshold, producing big batches but the async priority path occasionally schedules higher-priority flows that hijack worker slots. Requests already waiting without promoted age continue to wait longer — starvation.
- Age promotion and reserve slots break the adversarial sequence: promotion increases dispatch chance for long-wait requests; reserved slots give microbursts a fast lane without pushing older requests further back in the queue.

Implementation thoughts & safety checks:
- Age promotion logic is simple and contained; it requires careful tuning of promote_after_ms to avoid over-fragmentation of batches. Start with promote_after_ms = 10–15ms.
- Reserve slot should be configurable per-worker and per-tier (e.g., 0 for heavy-throughput workers, 1 for interactive-optimized). Validate under heavy GPU utilization to ensure no starvation of throughput-critical flows.
- Need rollout plan with feature flag and an automatic telemetry check: if p95/p99 increases more than X% after enabling, auto-disable.

Action items / next steps:
- [Sofia] Create a small PR to add promote_after_ms + metrics (histogram of queue-time by age buckets) — target: PR draft by 2025-03-10.
- [Ethan] Implement reserve_probe_slot config and e2e test that simulates microbursts — target: 2025-03-14.
- [Maya] Instrument more granular traces to link batch formation decisions to per-request metadata (route, origin) — target: 2025-03-12.
- Run multi-node variant of W4 on a small cluster to catch cross-node scheduling noise (blocked until PRs landed).

Open questions / things to watch:
- What is the right default promote_after_ms across regions? Latency characteristics differ between hosted and private deployments.
- Interplay with KV-cache warmup: promoted requests that trigger cache misses may still incur long tail; we should combine cache warmup metrics with age buckets.
- Can we opportunistically piggyback small requests on adjacent batch in-flight (speculative merge) without increasing p999?

Quick runbook snippets (bench-runner flags and config examples):
- bench-runner --workload microburst --qps 5 --burst 200 --burst-duration-ms 300 --interval-s 30 --seed 42
- runtime config snippet:
  scheduler: {
    max_wait_ms: 8,
    max_batch_tokens: 16384,
    promote_after_ms: 12,
    reserve_probe_slot: 1
  }

TL;DR:
- Purely increasing coalescence window buys batch size and tokens/s but can catastrophically increase p999 under microbursty low-QPS workloads.
- Two lightweight mitigations (age-based promotion and a single reserved slot per worker) reliably reduce tail latency for the cases we care about with minimal throughput cost.
- Recommend a small, staged rollout: add promote_after_ms metric + telemetry, then ship reserve_probe_slot behind a flag, run multi-node verification, and ship combined heuristics as opt-in defaults for interactive-optimized fleets.

Notes to self (scratchpile):
- Check impact of promote_after_ms on average batch fragmentation during peak load (daily night window).
- Add a ticket to correlate p999 spikes with route labels (some routes might be more sensitive).
- Cross-reference with incident logs: customer ABC-512 reported similar symptoms (link in JIRA-RT-4521).

End of doc.
